issues.title: Document instances where `go-git` diverges from upstream `git`
issues.body:
Map and document all instances where `go-git` may have a slightly different behaviour than upstream.
The documentation should clarify whether the drift is intentional (and why is that so) or whether that is something to be fixed at some point in time.

Some examples:

- [ ] **Cloning empty repositories**
  - Drift: returns `transport.ErrEmptyRemoteRepository` instead of initialising a new repository.
  - Resolution: Keep as is.
  - Reasoning: The current behaviour is better aligned to a library, as opposed to the behaviour `git` has which is a better fit for a cli. Additionally,`go-git` already provides an API that enable users to simulate upstream behaviour if/when needed.
  - xref: https://github.com/go-git/go-git/issues/118#issuecomment-1759167978
- [ ] **Reading and writing Git config**
  - Drift: TBC
  - Resolution: TBC
  - xref: https://github.com/go-git/go-git/issues/395
- [ ] **Shallow cloning**
  - Drift: When shallow cloning `go-git` defaults to fetching `AllTags`, resulting in a larger network traffic than `git`.
  - Resolution: TBC
  - xref: https://github.com/go-git/go-git/issues/545#issuecomment-1353681676

issues.title: `Worktree.Add` walks the entire worktree even when adding a single subdirectory
issues.body:
Adding a nested path costs a full worktree-vs-index diff. `doAdd` calls `w.Status()` for any directory path (and for files too, unless `SkipStatus` is set). Status goes through `diffStagingWithWorktree`, which builds the "to" side with `filesystem.NewRootNodeWithOptions(w.filesystem, …)`, that constructor takes no path or prefix, so the merkletrie diff always starts at the worktree root. `doAddDirectory` then iterates the whole status map and throws away everything that doesn't match via `isPathInDirectory`.

So `wt.Add("deeply/nested/dir")` scans the entire tree to keep a handful of entries. On a large repo this dominates the cost of Add, and it gets worse the bigger the repo and the more specific the path.

Upstream git just tightened the equivalent path in the other direction: https://github.com/git/git/commit/b6f17686b20647fc904e6201fa6d168731e588eb restores the common-prefix optimization when a leading `:(exclude)` item had been suppressing it, so git descends only the subtree the positive pathspecs share. We're missing the baseline optimization entirely, not just that edge case.

issues.title: index: feature.manyFiles / feature.experimental not expanded, so index.skipHash is ignored (invalid checksum on read)
issues.body:
### Bug Description

When a repository's `.git/config` enables `index.skipHash` indirectly via Git's
`feature.manyFiles = true` (or `feature.experimental = true`) meta-setting,
go-git fails to read the index with:

```
index decoder: invalid checksum
```

Git writes the index trailer as 20 (or 32 for SHA-256) zero bytes when
`index.skipHash` is in effect. go-git supports `index.skipHash` when the key is
present **literally** under `[index]`, but it does not expand Git's
`feature.*` aliases, so `Config.Index.SkipHash` stays unset and the decoder
verifies the checksum against the all-zero trailer and rejects the index.


### go-git Version

v6.0.0-alpha

### Steps to Reproduce

```sh
git init repo && cd repo
git config feature.manyFiles true   # implies index.skipHash=true in Git >= 2.40
echo hi > a.txt && git add a.txt && git commit -m init
```

```go
package main

import (
    "fmt"

    git "github.com/go-git/go-git/v6"
)

func main() {
    repo, err := git.PlainOpen("repo")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    wt, err := repo.Worktree()
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    _, err = wt.Status()
    fmt.Println("status err:", err) // => index decoder: invalid checksum
}
```

`git status` on the same repo works fine. Adding `git config index.skipHash true`
explicitly also makes go-git succeed, confirming the gap is alias expansion, not
checksum handling.


### Additional Information

### Expected behavior

go-git should honor Git's `feature.manyFiles` / `feature.experimental`
meta-settings, which expand to (per Git docs):

- `feature.manyFiles=true` → `index.skipHash=true`, `index.version=4`, `core.untrackedCache=true`
- `feature.experimental=true` → `index.skipHash=true` (among others)

so that reading such an index does not error. At minimum, `index.skipHash`
should be inferred from `feature.manyFiles` / `feature.experimental` when the
literal `index.skipHash` key is absent.

- `feature.manyFiles` is increasingly common: some Git

issues.title: Worktree.RemoveGlob does not remove directory
issues.body:
# Issue

When provided an exact path to a directory, `(*Worktree).RemoveGlob` fails to remove it. For example, `RemoveGlob("foo")` with the following working tree has no effect:

```
foo
    bar
    xyz
abc
baz
```

However, `RemoveGlob("fo*")` does work because the wildcard matches `foo/bar` and `foo/xyz` (and the empty directory gets subsequently deleted from the working tree).

Git works as expected; `git rm -r foo` deletes `foo` and its contents.

# Cause

This is at least partially caused by the fact that [`(*Index).Glob`](https://github.com/go-git/go-git/blob/9cf0e3ee57dd5e4cf97e9e45cfca7eeb460cc983/plumbing/format/index/index.go#L97) fails to resolve these sorts of globs. The original `filepath/path` implementation of `Glob` from which go-git's is taken does not run into this problem because it has more logic to traverse the filesystem instead of simply comparing full paths to the glob pattern.

It seems that `(*Worktree).RemoveGlob` would also require changes even if `(*Index).Glob` were to be changed, though, since it only attempts to delete files (and deletes empty directories after files.)

## Ideas

- As a partial solution, go-billy's `Glob` implementation can handle these sorts of patterns correctly. However, I don't think that will work for removing files which are present in the index but not the working tree?
- I'm not familiar enough with Git to know if changing `Index` to be a tree structure is a bad idea (or at least not worth the effort for this relatively small issue, unless it has positive effects elsewhere.)
- A possible hackfix would be to check if the given glob pattern is the exact path to a directory and append `/*` to the pattern.

issues.title: ObjectWriter creates files as mode 0600, even if core.sharedRepository = "group"
issues.body:
Per https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config, if `core.sharedRepository` = group, then "the repository is made shareable between several users in a group (making sure all the files and objects are group-writable)". This is useful when sharing an on-disk repo between two unix users (e.g. a web server, and a normal user accessing the repo via git push/pull over SSH).

go-git seems to unconditionally create object files as 0600, meaning they are unaccessible to members of the group.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a repository with `git init --shared` (this sets `core.sharedRepository` to `group`)
2. Commit via https://github.com/go-git/go-git/blob/master/_examples/commit/main.go

### Expected
Files created in `git/objects/` are at least group-readable, e.g. 0660.

### Actual
Files created in `.git/objects/` are 0600.

### What's happening

1. ObjectWriter uses billy.Filesystem's TempFile: https://github.com/go-git/go-git/blob/809f9df1b76258a311a20c76d346e86aca0a08f8/storage/filesystem/dotgit/writers.go#L256
2. billy.Filesystem's TempFile uses ioutil.TempFIle: https://github.com/src-d/go-billy/blob/780403cfc1bc95ff4d07e7b26db40a6186c5326e/osfs/os.go#L99
3. ioutil.TempFile uses 0600 https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.21.1:src/os/tempfile.go;l=44

## Summary

Make `plumbing/format/config.Config` the single data model for all git
configuration, replacing the higher-level `config` package's hard-coded
struct projection.  Add a typed query/mutation API that mirrors the
capabilities of the canonical `git config` command — including
git-specific value types (bool, int, path, color, expiry-date), typed
getters and setters, value-pattern matching for multi-valued keys, regex
key search, section rename, default values, and inline comments.

## Motivation

**Current API is string-only and ad-hoc.**

`format/config` stores every value as a raw `string`.  The higher-level
`config` package performs type coercion case-by-case using `strconv.ParseBool`,
which does not match git's keyword set.  There are no reusable typed accessors,
no value-pattern matching, and no canonicalisation on write.

**Incorrect bool parsing.**

Git accepts `yes`, `on`, `no`, `off`, non-zero integers, and bare keys (no `=`)
as booleans.  Go's `strconv.ParseBool` only accepts `true`/`false`/`1`/`0` and
their short forms.  This is a correctness gap that affects any consumer that
reads boolean config values.

**No integer suffix expansion.**

Git config values like `10M`, `1G`, `512k` are common (e.g.

**No multi-value discrimination.**

Git's `set --value=<pattern>`, `unset --value=<pattern>`, and `get --value=<pattern>`

replaces the first occurrence by key only; `RemoveOption` removes all values.

`git config get --regexp` finds all keys matching a regex.  go-git has no

`git config get --url=<URL>` resolves config scoped to a URL subsection

## Summary

When implementing a Git smart HTTP server with `plumbing/transport/server`, native `git push` fails if the server advertises common receive-pack capabilities (`side-band-64k`, `atomic`) and then handles the push with go-git's receive-pack session.

The request decodes successfully, but `ReceivePack` returns:

```
unsupported capability: side-band-64k
```

The git client then reports:

```
error: RPC failed; HTTP 500
send-pack: unexpected disconnect while reading sideband packet
fatal: the remote end hung up unexpectedly
```

## go-git version

`github.com/go-git/go-git/v5 v5.19.1`

## Root cause

`rpSession.setSupportedCapabilities` only advertises/supports:

- `agent`
- `ofs-delta`
- `delete-refs`
- `report-status`

However, smart HTTP servers commonly advertise additional receive-pack capabilities that native `git` clients will use when present, including:

- `side-band-64k`
- `atomic`

Upload-pack on the server side already supports sideband capabilities (`upSession.setSupportedCapabilities` sets `Sideband` and `Sideband64k`), but receive-pack does not.

A go-git HTTP/git server should be able to:

1. Advertise standard receive-pack capabilities used by native git clients
2. Accept a native `git push` over smart HTTP stateless RPC
3. Return a valid report-status response (including sideband encoding when negotiated)

- If the server advertises `side-band-64k`, native `git push` fails with `unsupported capability: side-band-64k`
- If the server advertises only the capabilities currently supported by `rpSession`, native `git push` succeeds and refs are updated correctly

Currently [`serveUploadPackV2`](https://github.com/go-git/go-git/blob/bb92758aceaac38bdea920a521e57407f626b42b/plumbing/transport/upload_pack.go#L452) seems to assume that each capability line is a command (aka. starts with `command=`) but, as far as I can understand the [git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitprotocol-v2#_capabilities), that may not always be the case because some git clients may also send non-command capabilities such as [`object-format=sha1`](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitprotocol-v2#_object_format).

	"os"
	"os/exec"

	git "github.com/go-git/go-git/v5"
)

	cmd := exec.Command("git", args...)
	cmd.Dir = dir

		"GIT_COMMITTER_NAME=t", "GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL=[email]")
	if out, err := cmd.CombinedOutput(); err != nil {
		panic(string(out))
	}
}

func main() {
	src, _ := os.MkdirTemp("", "src")
	run(src, "init", "-q", "-b", "master")
	os.WriteFile(src+"/prn.sh", []byte("echo hi\n"), 0644)

issues.title: plumbing: transport, Send the server's shallow boundary on v2 fetch from a shallow repository
issues.body:
When the repository `UploadPack` serves is itself shallow, a v2 `fetch` that sends no `shallow`, `deepen`, `deepen-since` or `deepen-not` gets no `shallow-info` section. The pack ends at the server's shallow commits, since their parents are not in the repository, but the client is never told those commits are its boundary. A client that then checks connectivity finds parents it does not have.

Git writes the section in that case as well: `send_shallow_info` runs when `is_repository_shallow()` holds and, when no deepen was requested, calls `deepen(INFINITE_DEPTH)` [1]. That reaches `get_shallows_or_depth`, which reports a commit grafted in the server's shallow file as a boundary commit at any depth [2], so a `deepen N` that reaches the server's boundary before depth N reports it too.

v0/v1 are not affected: `receive_needs` returns before sending any shallow lines unless the client sent a depth, a deepen or a shallow line [3].

Note that git as a client records the boundary commits it did not ask for only when cloning, and leaves `.git/shallow` alone on a plain fetch into a repository that has references; #2443 applies the same rule to go-git's client.

The current code notes the gap ("Serving from a shallow repository is not handled."); it came up in review of #2477 [4], and is the same on `main`.

[1]: https://github.com/git/git/blob/v2.55.0/upload-pack.c#L1747-L1761
[2]: https://github.com/git/git/blob/v2.55.0/shallow.c#L197-L200
[3]: https://github.com/git/git/blob/v2.55.0/upload-pack.c#L1186-L1187
[4]: https://github.com/go-git/go-git/pull/2477#discussion_r4179212563

issues.body:

After a sparse checkout (`CheckoutOptions.SparseCheckoutDirectories`), switching to another branch with `Worktree.Checkout` does not update the index entries outside the sparse directories. They keep the blobs of the branch that was checked out before, and entries for files that do not exist on the target branch are not removed.

HEAD does move to the target branch, so the stale entries become staged changes, and the next commit made from that worktree includes them: it carries the previous branch's content for every path outside the sparse directories.

git updates those entries on checkout (the skip-worktree bit stays set) and reports a clean status.

issues.title: Potential inconsistency when partial object writes occur during fetch: missing blobs may not be recovered
issues.body:
### Bug Description

In the current `fetch` implementation (e.g., in `remote.go`), the logic for determining which objects to request (`wants`) relies primarily on whether the **commit object** referenced by a remote ref exists locally:
https://github.com/go-git/go-git/blob/16e6d0af8b41d2a9920ddb0363cf9917ef6ed028/remote.go#L988

However, this approach assumes that if the commit object exists, then its entire object graph (tree, blobs, etc.) is also complete and valid.

This assumption can break in rare but possible scenarios — for example:
* During a previous `fetch`, the commit object was successfully written to `.git/objects/`, but a subsequent blob or tree object failed to write (e.g., due to disk full, I/O error, or process crash).
* The local repository now contains a dangling or incomplete object graph: the commit exists, but one or more of its referenced objects (tree/blob) are missing or corrupted.
* On the next `fetch`, since `objectExists` returns true for the commit, it is **not added t**o the `wants` list, and the missing dependent objects are never re-fetched.
* As a result, the repository remains in an inconsistent state, and operations like checkout or status may fail with "missing blob" or "corrupt tree" errors.

Question:
Should `go-git` enhance its `objectExists`-based logic to also **validate the integrity of the commit’s object graph** before deciding to skip it in wants? For example:
* Attempt to parse the commit and its root tree (without loading all blobs).
*  If any referenced object is missing, treat the commit as incomplete and include it in wants.

Thanks for considering this edge case! 

### go-git Version

v5.11.0

issues.body:
### Bug Description

On the filesystem storage, `CheckAndSetReference(new, old)` can have side effects when it fails.

When the reference has no loose file (it is packed, or doesn't exist) and `old` doesn't match, the call
correctly returns an error, but it leaves an **empty loose ref file** behind. From then on:

- `Repository.References()` / `IterReferences()` fails for the whole repository with `ref file is empty`,
- `git show-ref` fails with `fatal: bad ref`, and `git for-each-ref` warns and skips the ref.

A second, related problem: on filesystems without `billy.ReadAndWriteCapability`, the `old` check is
**skipped entirely** when the ref has no loose file, so a stale update is silently applied.

## Expected behaviour (reference git)

[`git update-ref <ref> <new> <old>`](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-update-ref) stores `<new>` "after
verifying that the current value of the `<ref>` matches `<old-oid>`". When the check fails, nothing
is written:

```
$ git update-ref refs/bugs/missing $B $A
fatal: update_ref failed for ref 'refs/bugs/missing': cannot lock ref 'refs/bugs/missing': unable to resolve reference 'refs/bugs/missing'

$ git update-ref refs/bugs/packed $A $A     # packed ref, currently at $B
fatal: update_ref failed for ref 'refs/bugs/packed': cannot lock ref 'refs/bugs/packed': is at 5a327ab... but expected 2b3edd5...
```

In both cases no loose file is created, and `git for-each-ref` still lists the packed ref.

Tracing git (2.47.3) shows why: it takes `refs/heads/topic.lock` (`O_CREAT|O_EXCL`), checks the current
value, and on mismatch unlinks the lock. On success it writes the lock file and renames it over the

issues.body:
## Bug Description

A depth-one fetch of multiple related refs can cause `PushContext` to reject an update that is unambiguously fast-forward.

Given this graph:

```text
R -- B -- C  refs/heads/flipt/staging-test/blocker
     |
     +------  refs/heads/staging-test
     |
     +------  refs/heads/flipt/staging-test/target
```

fetching `staging-test` and `flipt/staging-test/*` with `Depth: 1` records both `B` and `C` as shallow boundaries. If the client then creates `N` with `B` as its direct parent and pushes `N` over the target branch, go-git rejects the update with:

```text
non-fast-forward update: refs/heads/flipt/staging-test/target
```

Expected behavior: the push succeeds because `N` is a direct descendant of the advertised remote head `B`.

Actual behavior: go-git rejects the update locally as non-fast-forward before sending it to `git-receive-pack`.

The equivalent operation using native Git with the same depth-one refspecs and commit graph succeeds.

- `github.com/go-git/go-git/v6 v6.0.0-alpha.5`
- current `main`: `v6.0.0-alpha.5.0.20260907191556-57ed51864460`

git version 2.50.1 (Apple Git-155)

While auditing `plumbing/transport/http` we found three spots where a server/redirect-controlled string is embedded into an error message without going through the `bounded()`/`redactURL` machinery this package otherwise uses consistently to cap attacker-controlled input before rendering it into errors/logs. These aren't fetch-breaking — they're a hardening/consistency gap relative to the invariant the package already establishes elsewhere.

## 1. `Content-Type` header embedded unbounded in `describeInfoRefsError`

`plumbing/transport/http/handshake.go:336`: `mediaType` (derived from the response's `Content-Type` header via `contentMediaType`, which has no length cap) is embedded via `%q` into the returned error, unlike every other server-controlled string this package renders through `bounded()`.

A server or redirect target sending an oversized `Content-Type` header (bounded only by net/http's own multi-MB header size limit) gets that value embedded verbatim into the error message and any log/trace that prints it.

## 2. `redactURL` doesn't bound `u.Scheme`

`plumbing/transport/http/common.go:578`: `redactURL` bounds `Host`, `Path`, `RawQuery`, `Fragment`, and `User`, but never bounds or redacts `Scheme`, even though `net/url.Parse` places no length limit on it.

A misbehaving redirect target can send a `Location` header with an oversized scheme-like prefix (e.g. thousands of legal scheme characters before `://`). When a hop is refused (e.g. under `NoFollowRedirects`, or a scheme/host change `checkRedirect` rejects), `redactClientError`/`redactedURL` passes that oversized scheme straight through unbounded into the error message the caller receives — unlike every other URL component this function is designed to cap.

## 3. `applyRedirect` error branches print unbounded path/scheme

`plumbing/transport/http/common.go:247` (and ~250, ~265, ~269-271): several error branches print server-controlled `finalPath` and `final.Scheme`/`baseURL.Schem

`Commit.MergeBase` rebuilds an ancestor index on **every call**, so computing merge bases for N branches against one trunk re-walks the trunk N times — O(N × history). There is no way to amortise the shared side.

This is not a correctness bug; the results are right. It is a missing amortisation path for a common shape: "map many branches onto one mainline", which any forge, CI, or VCS tool built on go-git ends up doing.

Fixture: bare repo, 3000-commit trunk, **1000 branches** each forked at a random trunk commit with 2 commits of its own.

issues.title: plumbing/object: decoded commits lose ident and header byte fidelity
issues.body:
## Problem

Decoding and then structurally re-encoding a commit can change data that the caller did not mutate. Some losses change decoded values; others preserve the value but change the exact object bytes and therefore its ID and signed payload.

## Decode correctness

### `Signature.Decode` misreads an ident with no space before the date

`Signature.Decode` starts the timestamp at `closeBracket+2`, assuming exactly one space after the closing `>`:

```go
hasTime := closeBracket+2 < len(b)
if hasTime {
    s.decodeTimeAndTimeZone(b[closeBracket+2:])
}
```

For this ident:

```text
A U Thor <a@x>1700000000 +0000
```

go-git consumes the leading `1` as part of the assumed separator and parses Unix timestamp `700000000` instead of `1700000000`.

Git's complete [`split_ident_line`](https://github.com/git/git/blob/dea0ea3582e6980ddbc1173cc8e3e9f9db91cde0/ident.c#L275-L349) implementation parses the ident. The relevant [date-start logic](https://github.com/git/git/blob/dea0ea3582e6980ddbc1173cc8e3e9f9db91cde0/ident.c#L321-L329) advances past the closing `>`, skips zero or more whitespace characters, and records the timestamp start.

The same object reads correctly with Git:

```console
$ git hash-object -t commit -w --stdin --literally < obj
d800c86aa26c1bff1fcf10df813a505d4e6461d0
$ git log --format='%at | %ai' -1 d800c86
1700000000 | 2023-11-14 22:13:20 +0000
```

`git fsck` calls this shape `missingSpaceBeforeDate`, but Git reads it, and import/rewrite tools can produce it.

issues.title: gitignore: non-trailing `**` does not backtrack — `**/a/b` fails to match `a/x/a/b`
issues.body:
### Summary

In `plumbing/format/gitignore`, a non-trailing `**` locks onto the **first** path component that matches the segment following it. When a later segment then fails, the whole match is reported as a non-match instead of retrying the `**` expansion from the next candidate component. Real git backtracks here (wildmatch expands `**` recursively), so go-git disagrees with `git check-ignore` on common patterns like `**/a/b`.

### Expected behaviour

gitignore(5): *"A slash followed by two consecutive asterisks then a slash matches **zero or more directories**. For example, `a/**/b` matches `a/b`, `a/x/b`, `a/x/y/b` and so on."* — `**` is an existential "zero or more", so every possible expansion must be tried.

Verified against real git (2.48.1, same result on 2.39.5; these patterns keep `**` in the positions git documents, so they are unaffected by the `foo**/bar` wildmatch corner case git fixed in 2.52.0):

```console
$ git init -q repro && cd repro
$ echo '**/a/b' > .gitignore
$ git check-ignore -v a/x/a/b
.gitignore:1:**/a/b	a/x/a/b        # ignored
$ echo 'a/**/b/c' > .gitignore
$ git check-ignore -v a/b/x/b/c
.gitignore:1:a/**/b/c	a/b/x/b/c    # ignored
```

### Actual behaviour

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"strings"

	"github.com/go-git/go-git/v6/plumbing/format/gitignore"
)

func main() {
	for _, c := range []struct{ pattern, path string }{
		{"**/a/b", "a/x/a/b"},
		{"**/foo/bar", "foo/baz/foo/bar"},
		{"a/**/b/c", "a/b/x/b/c"},
		{"**/node_modules/lodash", "web/node_modules/x/node_modules/lodash"},
	} {
		p := gitignore.ParsePattern(c.pattern, nil)
		r := p.Match(strings.Split(c.path, "/"), false)
		fmt.Printf("%-24q vs %-42q => %v\n", c.pattern, c.path, r == gitignore.Exclude)
	}
}
```

```
"**/a/b"                 vs "a/x/a/b"                                  => false   // git: ignored
"**/foo/bar"             vs "foo/baz/foo/bar"                          => false   // git: ignored
"a/**/b/c"               vs "a/b/x/b/c"

`Worktree.Status()` has a write side effect. For every submodule that is
registered in the repository's `.git/config` (i.e. `git submodule init` has

```
Worktree.Status()

    → Submodule.Status()

issues.title: storage: support atomic compare-and-delete for references
issues.body:
### Feature Description

Add a storage primitive that atomically deletes a reference only if it still matches an expected value.

`ReferenceStorer` currently exposes:

```go
CheckAndSetReference(newRef, old *plumbing.Reference) error
RemoveReference(name plumbing.ReferenceName) error
```

These methods cannot safely express conditional deletion. Reading a ref before calling `RemoveReference` introduces a race: another process may update the ref between the read and the unconditional delete.

Git provides this behavior through:

```sh
git update-ref -d <ref> <old-oid>
```

A possible API shape would be:

```go
CheckAndRemoveReference(old *plumbing.Reference) error
```

The operation should delete the ref only when its current value matches `old`; otherwise it should return a no-write reference-changed error.

### Feature Description

`go-git` defines two different interfaces to represent storers: [storage.Storer](https://github.com/go-git/go-git/blob/b5117ad1603d4a44b05d7b4d661b8e1e9d035518/storage/storer.go#L20) and [storer.Storer](https://github.com/go-git/go-git/blob/b5117ad1603d4a44b05d7b4d661b8e1e9d035518/plumbing/storer/storer.go#L6). The former is a more comprehensive abstraction, covering additional aspects of a "storer" for Git repositories, for example: submodules, config, shallow and index information.

As part of the [SHA256 implementation](https://github.com/go-git/go-git/pull/1825), additional interfaces (`storer.ObjectFormatGetter` and `storage.ObjectFormatSetter`) were created to avoid expanding the existing interfaces, which would lead to breaking backwards compatibility with existing off-tree Storer implementations. The stand-alone interfaces enable the in-tree logic to detect support for other `ObjectFormat` values while failing safe to avoid data corruption.

During the review of the interfaces we should consider potentially integrating the `ObjectFormat` requirements into then. It will make sense to break backwards compatibility then, as that version aims to [align with Git v3](https://github.com/go-git/go-git/issues/1831), which intends on making `SHA256` the default `ObjectFormat`.

issues.body:
### Feature Description

Creating a new linked worktree (or checking out a branch) currently decompresses every file from the object store, even when most files are already materialized in an existing worktree. This is the same approach used by Git C's git worktree add (which runs git reset --hard internally), but Git C compensates with parallel checkout workers and streaming blob writes — optimizations go-git currently lacks.

For large repositories, this makes worktree creation and clone checkout significantly slower than necessary.

#### Background

When git worktree add -b feature HEAD is executed, the new branch points to the **same commit** as the source. Every file in the target tree is byte-for-byte identical to the existing worktree. Despite this, both Git C and go-git decompress every blob from the object store individually.

Git C mitigates this with:
- **Parallel checkout** (parallel-checkout.c) — multiple worker processes write files concurrently.
- **Streaming blob writes** (odb_stream_blob_to_fd) — blobs stream directly to disk without full memory buffering.
- **Cache-tree fast path** (traverse_by_cache_tree) — skips entire subtrees when the index cache-tree matches the target tree OID.
- **CE_UPTODATE / FSMonitor** — avoids redundant lstat calls for files known to be clean.

- r.Config() is called inside copyObjectToWorktree for **every file** to check AutoCRLF.
- When AutoCRLF is enabled, each blob is decompressed **twice** (once for binary detection, once for writing).

issues.body:
